title: Boom, Bust and a Brand-New Economy
summary: In the 1990s people started using the Internet to buy books, sell old toys, bank, learn and chat face to face across oceans. Investors got so excited that they poured money into almost any company with '.com' in its name, until the bubble went POP in 2000. But the best ideas survived, and some of the most useful things online, like Wikipedia and Linux, were built by volunteers for free.

sections.heading: A Bookshop With No Shelves
paragraphs: In the spring of 1994, a 30-year-old computer scientist named Jeff Bezos was working at a New York investment firm called D. E. Shaw. He came across a striking number: use of the World Wide Web was growing at a rate of more than 2,000 percent a year. Bezos decided that something growing that fast was a chance he could not ignore. He made a list of products that might sell well online and picked books.

Why books? A normal bookshop, even a huge one, can only hold perhaps 100,000 or so different titles on its shelves. But millions of different books were in print. A website does not need shelves. It can list every book that exists and then order the right copy from a warehouse once a customer has paid. Books were also easy to describe, easy to post, and every copy of a particular book is identical, so customers did not need to touch them before buying.

Bezos quit his job, and he and his wife MacKenzie moved across the United States to the Seattle area. Seattle had plenty of skilled computer programmers and was close to a big book distribution warehouse in Roseburg, Oregon. On 5 July 1994 he founded the company in Bellevue, Washington, working out of the garage of a rented house. Its first name was Cadabra, as in 'abracadabra', but people kept hearing it as 'cadaver', which is a dead body. By November he had renamed it Amazon, after the river that carries more water than any other on Earth. The name suggested something enormous, and it also came near the top of alphabetical lists.

The website opened to the public on 16 July 1995 and boldly called itself 'Earth's Biggest Bookstore'. The tiny team built desks out of wooden doors screwed onto legs, because doors were cheaper than real desks. In the early days a bell rang every time an order came in, until there were so many orders that the ringing became unbearable and the bell was switched off. Within its first two months, orders arrived from every US state and from more than 45 other countries. One of the very first books bought is often said to have been a book about how computers might think up ideas, called 'Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies' by Douglas Hofstadter.

Amazon sold shares to the public on the stock market in May 1997. Soon it was selling music and videos, then toys, electronics and almost anything else. Yet for years it made no profit at all, because it spent every dollar on growing. Its first profitable quarter did not come until the end of 2001. Many people laughed at it as an example of a company that was all hype. As you will see, the laughter turned out to be premature.

sections.heading: A Broken Laser Pointer and a Pez Tale
paragraphs: Amazon sold new things. A different idea was to help ordinary people sell things to each other. On the Labor Day weekend of 1995, a 28-year-old French-born Iranian-American programmer called Pierre Omidyar wrote some code at his home in San Jose, California, and launched a page called AuctionWeb. It was a hobby, a side project on his personal website. Anyone could list an item, and other people could bid for it, just like at an auction, except the auction lasted days and the bidders could be anywhere in the world.

One of the first things Omidyar listed was a broken laser pointer. To his amazement, it sold for 14 dollars and 83 cents. He emailed the buyer to make sure they understood that it did not work. The buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. Omidyar realised that the Internet could connect people with very unusual interests: somewhere out there, for almost anything, there was someone who wanted it.

AuctionWeb made about 1,000 dollars in its first month, mostly from small fees on sales. Soon it was so busy that Omidyar's web host made him upgrade to a business account, and he began charging sellers properly. He hired his first employee, Chris Agarpao, and then a president, Jeff Skoll. In September 1997 the site was renamed eBay. The name came from Omidyar's consulting company, Echo Bay Technology Group. He had wanted echobay.com, but a gold-mining company already had it, so he shortened it to eBay.com. In March 1998 Meg Whitman became chief executive, and that September eBay sold shares to the public. On their first day the shares jumped from 18 dollars to 53 dollars.

You may have heard that eBay was started so that Omidyar's girlfriend (later his wife) could trade Pez sweet dispensers with other collectors. It is a charming story, but it is not how eBay began. It was invented in 1997 by a member of eBay's public relations team, who thought reporters would find a love story about sweet dispensers more interesting than a programmer experimenting with an auction website. She was right: newspapers repeated it for years. It is a good example of why historians check where a story first came from.

eBay had a real problem to solve: how could strangers trust each other? A buyer in Texas might send money to a seller in Scotland and never receive the item. eBay's answer was the feedback system. After each sale, buyer and seller could rate each other as positive, neutral or negative and leave a comment. Over time, each person built a public score, a reputation. Honest sellers with hundreds of happy customers became trusted. This idea of ratings from strangers spread everywhere: today taxi apps, holiday rentals and online shops all use descendants of it.

Paying was the other headache. Early eBay buyers often posted paper cheques or money orders, which took days. A company called PayPal made it possible to pay by email address, and it became so popular among eBay users that eBay bought PayPal in October 2002 for about 1.4 billion dollars.

sections.heading: The Gold Rush: The Dot-Com Boom
paragraphs: To understand what happened next, you need to know a little about shares. When a company 'goes public', it sells small pieces of itself, called shares or stocks, on a stock market. People buy shares hoping the company will grow and the shares will become worth more. The price of a share depends on what buyers believe the company will be worth in the future, not just on what it earns today. That means excitement can push prices very high, and fear can push them very low.

Many people date the start of the boom to 9 August 1995. That day Netscape, the company that made the popular Netscape Navigator browser you met in Part 11, sold its shares to the public. They had been priced at 28 dollars each, but so many people wanted them that on the first day they shot up to around 75 dollars before settling at about 58. Netscape had barely made any profit. Suddenly the whole world noticed that a young Internet company could be worth billions on paper.

Over the next five years, investors rushed to buy shares in anything connected to the Internet. New companies were called 'dot-coms', because their names often ended in '.com'. Many of them had a simple plan called 'get big fast': spend huge amounts of money on advertising to attract as many visitors, or 'eyeballs', as possible, and worry about making a profit later. Some companies added '.com' to their names, and their share price jumped just because of it.

The NASDAQ is a US stock market index (a kind of average) that includes lots of technology companies. It rose by several hundred percent between 1995 and early 2000. In January 2000, the American football Super Bowl showed more than a dozen adverts from dot-com companies (counts range from about 12 to 19), and each 30-second advert cost around 2 million dollars. The same month, the online service AOL announced it would merge with the giant media company Time Warner, the biggest merger in history at that time. It seemed as if Internet companies were about to swallow the old world.

Some of the new companies were brilliant ideas that were simply too early. Webvan delivered groceries ordered online and built huge, expensive automated warehouses before it had enough customers. Pets.com sold pet food and supplies online, and became famous for its talking sock-puppet mascot. The trouble was that heavy bags of dog food are expensive to ship, and the company often sold items for less than they cost to buy and deliver. A European fashion website called Boo.com spent well over 100 million dollars in less than two years.

Telephone and cable companies joined the rush too. They believed Internet traffic would keep doubling at incredible speeds, so they borrowed hundreds of billions of dollars and laid enormous amounts of new fibre-optic cable, the glass threads you met in Part 13. Much of it was never switched on at first. Engineers called the unused strands 'dark fibre'.

sections.heading: Pop! The Bubble Bursts
paragraphs: Imagine blowing a soap bubble. It grows bigger and shinier, but the skin gets thinner and thinner. Economists use the word 'bubble' for a time when prices climb far above what things are really worth, because sooner or later the skin breaks.

On 10 March 2000 the NASDAQ index reached 5,048.62, the highest it had ever been. Then it started to fall. At first people hoped it was just a wobble. It was not. Investors began asking awkward questions: when will these companies actually make money? Many of them were spending their investors' cash so fast that they would run out within months. Once a few big investors started selling, others panicked and sold too, and prices tumbled.

The fall lasted more than two years. By October 2002 the NASDAQ had lost about 78 percent of its value from the peak. That means a share worth 100 dollars at the top might have been worth only about 22 dollars at the bottom. Estimates suggest investors lost around 5 trillion dollars on paper. Pets.com closed in November 2000, only nine months after selling its shares to the public. Webvan went bankrupt in 2001. Thousands of people who had joined exciting start-ups found themselves out of work.

Even strong companies were battered. Amazon's share price fell by more than 90 percent between late 1999 and 2001, and newspapers wondered whether it would survive. It did, by cutting costs and focusing on customers, and it finally reported a profit for a whole year in 2003. eBay, which charged fees on every sale and so made real money from the start, kept growing through the crash. Google, founded in 1998, was still a small private company and quietly kept improving its search engine.

The NASDAQ did not climb back above its March 2000 high until 2015, fifteen years later. Yet the crash did not mean the Internet had failed. People did not stop emailing, shopping or searching. What failed was the idea that any website with a catchy name would automatically become rich. A study of the period found that about half of the dot-com companies were still in business in 2004, usually smaller and humbler.

The bust even left behind useful gifts. All that dark fibre laid by bankrupt telecom companies was still in the ground. Other companies bought it cheaply, and in the following years it carried the floods of video, music and photos that people began sharing. Some of the Internet's later success was built on the leftovers of its first great crash.

sections.heading: Banking, Booking and Homework: Daily Life Moves Online
paragraphs: While the stock market rose and fell, ordinary life was quietly changing. In 1994, a group of pizza restaurants in Santa Cruz, California tested a service called PizzaNet that let people order Pizza Hut pizza through a web page. Around the same time, Stanford Federal Credit Union is often credited with offering some of the first Internet banking to its members. In 1995 Security First Network Bank opened as one of the first banks that existed only online, with no branches at all.

Online banking meant you could check your balance at midnight, move money between accounts, or pay a bill without queuing at a counter. To make it safe, banks relied on the encryption you will meet in Part 17, which scrambles information so that people snooping on the network cannot read it. At first many customers were nervous about typing bank details into a computer. Within about a decade, millions of people did it every day, and today many banks have closed branches because so few customers visit.

Travel changed just as much. Before the Internet, booking a flight usually meant phoning an airline or visiting a travel agent, who looked up seats on a special computer system that ordinary people could not use. In 1996 Microsoft launched Expedia, and other travel websites followed. Suddenly anyone could compare prices from many airlines and hotels at once. Booking concert tickets, cinema seats and train journeys moved online in the same way.

School and libraries changed too. Libraries replaced wooden drawers full of index cards with online catalogues, so you could find out from home whether a book was on the shelf. Project Gutenberg, started by Michael Hart back in 1971, typed up books that were old enough to be free of copyright and shared them online, and by the 2000s it offered thousands of free e-books. Pupils who once relied on a printed encyclopedia at home could now look up information on the Web, although, as Part 12 warned, they also had to learn to judge whether it was trustworthy.

Work began to move as well. Email replaced many letters and faxes. Some people started working from home a few days a week, sending files over the Internet instead of carrying them into an office. Companies discovered they could hire a programmer in India or a designer in Poland as easily as one down the street. During the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020, these habits were tested on a giant scale, when hundreds of millions of children around the world attended school through screens for weeks or months. Not everyone benefited equally, though: people without a computer or a good connection were left out, a problem Part 18 explores.

sections.heading: An Encyclopedia Anyone Can Edit
paragraphs: In March 2000, an Internet entrepreneur named Jimmy Wales and a philosophy PhD named Larry Sanger started an online encyclopedia called Nupedia. It was free to read, but it worked like a traditional encyclopedia: experts wrote articles, and each article went through a long, careful review by other experts. That was good for accuracy but painfully slow. After about a year, only a tiny number of articles had been completed.

Sanger heard about a kind of website called a wiki. The first wiki, WikiWikiWeb, had been created in 1995 by a programmer named Ward Cunningham. He named it after the 'Wiki Wiki' shuttle buses at Honolulu airport in Hawaii; 'wiki' is a Hawaiian word meaning 'quick'. On a wiki, any visitor can click 'edit' on a page, change it and save it immediately. Every earlier version is kept, so mistakes and vandalism can be undone.

On 10 January 2001 Sanger suggested using a wiki as a side project to feed draft articles into Nupedia. Five days later, on 15 January 2001, Wikipedia went live. The name joins 'wiki' and 'encyclopedia'. Wales is credited with the goal of a free encyclopedia anyone could edit, and Sanger with proposing the wiki method and leading the early community; the two later disagreed about who deserved how much credit, and Sanger left the project in 2002.

The side project quickly swallowed the main one. Thousands of volunteers began writing about everything from black holes to Bulgarian folk dances. Editions in other languages started in March 2001, and by the end of 2004 there were 161 of them. The English edition passed 2 million articles in 2007, and today it has more than 7 million, while Wikipedia as a whole exists in over 300 languages. Since 2003 it has been run by a non-profit charity, the Wikimedia Foundation, and it is paid for mostly by small donations rather than adverts.

How can an encyclopedia that anyone can change be reliable? Wikipedia's volunteers built rules and habits to help. Articles should take a 'neutral point of view' and every important fact should be backed up by a published, reliable source, listed in the footnotes. Editors watch lists of pages for changes, and automatic programs called bots spot obvious vandalism, like a page replaced with rude words, and reverse it within seconds. Every disagreement is argued out on a 'talk page' next to the article, so anyone can see why a decision was made.

In 2005 the science journal Nature asked experts to check a sample of science articles from Wikipedia and from the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Both had errors, and the experts found only somewhat more in Wikipedia than in Britannica. Britannica disputed the study's methods, and the argument made headlines. Most teachers today give a sensible middle answer: Wikipedia is a great place to start learning about a topic, but for important work you should follow its footnotes to the original sources and check them yourself.

sections.heading: Free Code for Everyone: Linux and Apache
paragraphs: Wikipedia was not the first big project built by volunteers sharing their work. Programmers had been doing it for years. To see how, you need to know about the 'kernel'. Every computer runs an operating system, the master program that starts when you switch it on and shares out the processor, memory and screen among all the other programs. At the very heart of the operating system is the kernel, the part that talks directly to the hardware.

In 1991 a 21-year-old student at the University of Helsinki in Finland, Linus Torvalds, bought a new PC and wanted to run a Unix-style operating system on it. The good ones were expensive, so he started writing his own kernel. On 25 August 1991 he posted a message to an online discussion group called comp.os.minix. He described it as 'just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu'. GNU was a project, begun by Richard Stallman in 1983, to create a complete free operating system, and it had produced many tools but did not yet have a working kernel of its own. Torvalds' kernel fitted the gap.

Torvalds wanted to call it Freax, but the administrator of the computer where he uploaded the files named the folder 'Linux', and the name stuck. In 1992 he released it under the GNU General Public License. This licence says that anyone may use, copy, study and change the code for free, as long as they share their improvements under the same rules. Programmers all over the world began sending in fixes and new features, using the Internet itself to coordinate their work. In 1996 Linux got its famous mascot, a cheerful penguin named Tux.

This way of working became known in 1998 as 'open source': the source code, the human-readable instructions of a program, is open for anyone to read and improve. It sounds as if it could never work. Why would people give away their work? Some did it for fun or to learn, some to build a reputation, and many because their employers found it cheaper to improve a shared version than to build a private one.

The results were astonishing. Linux now runs a huge share of the servers that power websites and online services. Since 2017, every one of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers has run Linux. And Android, the most widely used phone operating system on Earth, is built on the Linux kernel, so a hobby from a student's bedroom in Finland is now inside billions of pockets.

The Web had its own open-source hero. In early 1995 the most popular web server program was one written by Rob McCool at the NCSA in Illinois, the same centre that made the Mosaic browser. When McCool left, development stopped, so webmasters began swapping their own fixes, called 'patches', by email. In February 1995 eight of them formed the Apache Group, combined their patches, and released Apache 1.0 on 1 December 1995. In less than a year it became the most popular web server on the Internet, according to the Netcraft surveys that counted web servers, and it stayed on top for many years. People often joke that the name is a pun on 'a patchy server', because it was built from patches.

sections.heading: Songs, Lawsuits and Calls Across the World
paragraphs: Music was one of the first things to be turned upside down. A song on a CD takes up a lot of data, far too much to download over a dial-up modem. But a format called MP3 could squeeze a song to roughly a tenth of its size by throwing away sounds that human ears barely notice. A three-minute song became a file of about 3 megabytes, which a university network or a fast home connection could download in minutes.

In June 1999 a college student named Shawn Fanning, working with Sean Parker, launched Napster. It was a peer-to-peer program, which means that instead of downloading songs from one central website, users downloaded them directly from each other's computers. Napster just kept a giant list of who had which song. Type in the name of a band, and you could find almost any song ever recorded, including rare live recordings, for free. Students loved it. At its peak in February 2001 it had about 26 million users.

The problem was that most of the songs were copied without permission from the musicians and record companies who owned them, which is against copyright law. Record labels sued Napster in December 1999 in a case known as A&M Records v. Napster. In 2000 the heavy metal band Metallica and the rapper Dr. Dre sued too, after finding their unreleased songs being shared. Some musicians defended Napster as a way for fans to discover music, while others said it was simply taking their work without paying. In July 2001, following a court order, Napster shut down its network.

Napster lost, but it had proved that people wanted music instantly over the Internet. In April 2003 Apple opened the iTunes Music Store, selling legal downloads for 99 cents a song. A few years later, streaming services, which you will meet in Part 19, let people listen to millions of songs for a monthly fee or with adverts, without owning the files at all. The music business today earns much of its money from streaming, a model that grew out of the chaos Napster started.

Distance itself was shrinking too. In August 2003 a small team released the first public test version of Skype. It was founded by Niklas Zennström from Sweden and Janus Friis from Denmark, and the software was written by Estonian programmers Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu, Jaan Tallinn and Toivo Annus. The name came from 'sky' and 'peer-to-peer'. Skype turned a person's voice into packets and sent them over the Internet, so a call from London to Sydney cost nothing beyond the Internet connection, while an ordinary long-distance phone call could cost a lot per minute.

Soon Skype added video calls through a webcam. For families split between countries, it was life-changing: grandparents could watch a grandchild take first steps on a screen, and soldiers and sailors far from home could see their children's faces. eBay bought Skype in 2005 for about 2.6 billion dollars, and Microsoft bought it in 2011 for 8.5 billion. Skype itself was finally retired in May 2025, with users moved to Microsoft Teams, but by then video calling had become something billions of people did without a second thought.

By the end of the 2000s, the shape of a new economy was clear. Shopping, money, music, knowledge and conversation had all moved online, built by companies, by volunteers, and by a few rule-breakers. But almost all of it still had a familiar pattern: a company or an organised project made the content, and everyone else read, watched or bought it. A new idea was about to flip that around. What if ordinary people, not companies, created most of what was on the Web?

deepDive: Economists still argue about why the dot-com bubble grew so large. One explanation is 'irrational exuberance', a phrase used by US Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan in a speech in December 1996: investors convinced themselves that old rules about profits no longer applied to a 'New Economy'. Another points to cheap borrowing, to the many ordinary people trading shares online for the first time through cheap Internet brokers, and to the way bankers earned large fees for bringing new companies to the stock market. A third view says investors were not entirely foolish: they were right that the Internet would change everything, but wrong about which companies would win and how quickly. The numbers are dramatic. The NASDAQ Composite rose several hundred percent between 1995 and its close of 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000, then lost about 78 percent by October 2002, wiping out an estimated 5 trillion dollars of paper wealth. By November 2000 Internet stocks alone had fallen about 75 percent from their highs. Telecom equipment makers had invested over 500 billion dollars, largely with borrowed money, in the five years after the US Telecommunications Act of 1996. Yet roughly half of dot-com firms still existed in 2004, and the survivors, Amazon and eBay among them, turned out to be far more valuable than their peak prices suggested. Historians of technology note a recurring pattern, seen also in the British 'railway mania' of the 1840s: a genuine new network attracts a speculative frenzy, the frenzy collapses, and the over-built infrastructure is then used cheaply by the next generation. Open source raises its own debates. Economists once struggled to explain why skilled programmers would donate work worth millions. Studies point to a mix of motives: learning, reputation that leads to jobs, the satisfaction of solving problems, and companies' self-interest in sharing the cost of common tools. Wikipedia's reliability is likewise debated; its strength is transparency, since every edit and argument is public, but coverage is uneven, and topics favoured by its mostly volunteer editors receive more attention than others.
funFact: The first item sold on eBay's predecessor, AuctionWeb, was a broken laser pointer that went for 14 dollars and 83 cents to a buyer who said he collected broken laser pointers.
